summary: Colfosceril palmitate (Exosurf Neonatal) is a synthetic, protein-free pulmonary surfactant of dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) combined with cetyl alcohol and tyloxapol. It is instilled intratracheally through the endotracheal tube to prevent and treat respiratory distress syndrome (RDS, hyaline membrane disease) in premature infants by replacing deficient endogenous surfactant, lowering alveolar surface tension, and improving lung compliance and oxygenation. Each dose is 5 mL/kg (67.5 mg/kg phospholipid) delivered as two 2.5 mL/kg aliquots. Prophylaxis is given soon after birth with repeat doses at 12 and 24 hours; rescue therapy uses two doses 12 hours apart. Acute oxygenation may improve rapidly, requiring prompt reduction of ventilator/oxygen settings to avoid hyperoxia and pneumothorax. It is administered only by clinicians trained in neonatal intubation and ventilation, with continuous monitoring; key acute hazards include pulmonary hemorrhage, apnea, mucus plugging of the endotracheal tube, and transient bradycardia/desaturation during dosing.
indications: Prophylaxis of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in premature infants at high risk (e.g., birth weight <1350 g, or >1350 g with evidence of pulmonary immaturity), given as soon as possible after birth
Rescue (treatment) of infants with established RDS confirmed by chest radiograph and requiring mechanical ventilation

dosage.t: First dose as soon as possible after birth; repeat doses at 12 and 24 hours to infants remaining on mechanical ventilation (up to 3 doses total)
dosage.n: Reconstitute before use; confirm correct ETT position; deliver each half-dose with the infant positioned to aid distribution

admin: For intratracheal use only - administer through the endotracheal tube by clinicians experienced in neonatal intubation and ventilatory management
Reconstitute the lyophilized powder with the supplied diluent (preservative-free sterile water) immediately before use to form the suspension
Confirm proper ETT placement (auscultation, chest expansion, +/- radiograph) before dosing
Give the dose as two 2.5 mL/kg aliquots (half-doses), turning/positioning the infant between aliquots to promote even distribution to both lungs
Instill each aliquot in small bursts timed with inspiration, allowing recovery between bursts; avoid suctioning the ETT for ~2 hours after dosing unless airway obstruction occurs
Monitor heart rate, color, chest expansion, oxygen saturation, and ventilator pressures continuously during and after administration; pause dosing for marked bradycardia or desaturation
As lung compliance and oxygenation improve, promptly reduce peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP, and FiO2 to avoid hyperoxia, hypocarbia, and pulmonary air leak
moa: Colfosceril palmitate replaces deficient endogenous pulmonary surfactant in the immature lung. Its principal phospholipid, dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), adsorbs to the alveolar air-liquid interface and lowers surface tension; cetyl alcohol acts as a spreading agent and tyloxapol disperses the phospholipid. By reducing alveolar surface tension, it stabilizes alveoli against collapse at end-expiration, improves lung compliance and functional residual capacity, and thereby improves oxygenation and reduces the work of breathing in respiratory distress syndrome.

absolute: No absolute contraindications for the indicated emergency use in premature infants with RDS or at risk for RDS
relative: Active pulmonary hemorrhage (weigh risk; surfactant has been associated with pulmonary hemorrhage)
Congenital anomalies incompatible with life or known lethal pulmonary malformations (clinical judgment)
monitor: Continuous heart rate and oxygen saturation during dosing
Chest expansion and breath sounds for ETT obstruction/malposition
Arterial blood gases and ventilator settings after dosing

preg: Not applicable - colfosceril palmitate is administered directly to the neonate's lungs, not to the pregnant patient. No maternal exposure occurs.
lact: Not applicable - the drug is given to the neonate by the intratracheal route, not to the breastfeeding mother; there is no relevance to milk transfer.
renal: Not applicable - this is a neonatal intratracheal surfactant with negligible systemic absorption; no renal dose adjustment is made.
hepatic: Not applicable - this is a neonatal intratracheal surfactant; phospholipid components are taken up and recycled within the lung, and no hepatic dose adjustment is made.

major: No systemic drug interactions are expected (local intratracheal phospholipid with minimal systemic absorption)
interactions.diagnostics: No known interference with laboratory tests; serial arterial blood gases and chest radiographs guide therapy and ventilator weaning.

common: Transient bradycardia and oxygen desaturation during instillation
Mucus plugging of the endotracheal tube
Decrease in transcutaneous oxygen saturation during dosing
serious: Pulmonary hemorrhage (more frequent in the smallest, most premature infants)
Pneumothorax / pulmonary air leak (especially if ventilator settings are not reduced as compliance improves)
Patent ductus arteriosus / apnea of prematurity (associated with the underlying condition)
rare: Mucus plug causing complete endotracheal tube obstruction
Reflux of surfactant into the endotracheal tube
emergency: Acute endotracheal tube obstruction (mucus plugging) with desaturation
Severe sustained bradycardia or desaturation during dosing requiring interruption and resuscitation

monitoring: Continuous pulse oximetry (SpO2) / transcutaneous oxygen throughout and after each dose
Continuous heart rate and clinical color during instillation - pause for marked bradycardia or desaturation
Chest wall expansion and breath sounds bilaterally to confirm distribution and detect ETT obstruction or malposition
Frequent arterial blood gases to track oxygenation and ventilation
Ventilator settings (FiO2, peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP) - wean promptly as oxygenation and compliance improve to avoid hyperoxia and air leak
Chest radiograph for air leak, ETT position, and resolution of RDS
counsel: Surfactant is a medicine that coats the inside of your baby's lungs to help the tiny air sacs stay open so your baby can breathe and get oxygen more easily
It is given through the breathing tube in the NICU by the neonatal team, who watch your baby's heart rate and oxygen the whole time
Your baby may need it once for prevention soon after birth or repeated over the first day, depending on how the lungs respond
As the lungs improve, the team will lower the ventilator and oxygen settings - this is a good sign, not a setback
The team monitors for side effects such as bleeding in the lungs or the tube becoming blocked and treats these immediately
Ask the NICU staff any questions about your baby's breathing support and progress
pk: Improvement in oxygenation and lung compliance often within minutes to a few hours of instillation
Maximal effect on oxygenation typically within hours; effect may require repeat dosing
Not characterized systemically; DPPC is taken up by type II pneumocytes and recycled within the alveolar surfactant pool
Surfactant effect persists for hours; repeat doses given at 12-24 h intervals as needed
Store lyophilized vials at controlled room temperature; reconstitute immediately before use and discard unused suspension
pearls: Oxygenation can improve rapidly after dosing - reduce FiO2 and ventilator pressures promptly to avoid hyperoxia, hypocarbia, and pneumothorax
Give the dose as two aliquots with repositioning to distribute surfactant to both lungs
Watch for mucus plugging of the endotracheal tube; avoid routine suctioning for about 2 hours after dosing unless obstruction occurs
Pulmonary hemorrhage is a recognized hazard, particularly in the smallest premature infants
Administer only in a NICU setting by clinicians skilled in neonatal intubation and ventilation, with continuous monitoring
Transient bradycardia and desaturation during instillation are common - pause and allow recovery, then resume
missed: Not applicable in the usual sense - dosing is a fixed prophylaxis or rescue schedule managed by the NICU team. If a scheduled repeat dose is delayed by clinical instability, the team gives it when the infant is stable and still intubated, within the labeled dosing window.
overdose: Acute overdosage has not been reported. Excessive instilled volume can cause airway obstruction and impaired gas exchange. If overdose or airway obstruction occurs, suction the endotracheal tube and provide supportive ventilatory care; manage bradycardia and desaturation with standard neonatal resuscitation. There is no specific antidote.
